name: Pectus excavatum / carinatum correction

lead: Pectus excavatum is a chest wall shape in which the breastbone and ribs sit inward (a 'funnel' or sunken chest); pectus carinatum is the opposite, with the sternum and ribs pushed outward ('pigeon chest'). Because the chest is the centrepiece of an upper-body physique, people who have either shape often look into correction to get a flatter, more symmetric torso that shirts and muscle development sit on more evenly.

Correction ranges from camouflage (clothing, muscle building, custom implants or fat grafting) to non-surgical devices (a vacuum bell for excavatum, a compression brace for carinatum) to operations such as the Nuss procedure, the Ravitch procedure and the reverse Nuss. Surgical literature on these is large, dating back to Ravitch's 1949 report and Nuss's minimally invasive technique first described in the 1990s.

paras: In practice the path starts with an assessment by a paediatric or thoracic surgeon, who measures severity (for example with a CT-derived Haller index) and checks flexibility of the chest. For carinatum in a growing teenager with a flexible chest, custom bracing worn for many hours a day over months is the usual first step. For excavatum, options include watching and exercise, a suction-cup vacuum bell, or a minimally invasive repair in which a curved steel bar is placed under the sternum and later removed. Adults or asymmetric cases may be offered an open repair or cosmetic implants.

Surgical repair involves significant postoperative pain, a hospital stay, and possible complications such as bar displacement, air or fluid around the lung, infection and recurrence; open and bar-based procedures carry different risk profiles. Braces require consistent long-term wear and work best in young, flexible chests. Online guides that promise to fix the deformity with exercise or posture alone are discussed in forums; clinical sources describe exercise as supportive rather than as a replacement for bracing or surgery.

angle.text: Correction changes the underlying chest wall shape rather than disguising it, which is why people with either deformity pursue it for a more even torso outline. Others use muscle building, custom silicone implants or fat grafting to camouflage the contour.

lead: Pectus excavatum (funnel chest) and pectus carinatum (pigeon chest) are congenital chest wall shapes in which the sternum and costal cartilages sit inward or project outward. Correction refers to the set of approaches used to change that shape: bracing and suction devices, surgical repairs, and cosmetic camouflage. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities the topic comes up as a frame and physique issue, because the chest outline affects how a torso looks in clothes and how pectoral muscle development reads.[1][2]

Excavatum is the more common form and is estimated to affect roughly 1 in 150 to 1 in 1,000 births, with males affected about three times as often as females; carinatum is rarer and also more frequent in males.[3][4] Reviews describe a likely genetic component and an overgrowth or growth disturbance of the costal cartilages as the leading hypothesis for both shapes.[2]

The Ravitch operation (1949) and the minimally invasive Nuss procedure (reported from a 1987 start, with a 10-year review published in 1998) are the best-known surgical techniques, and bracing is the first-line non-surgical option for carinatum in flexible, growing chests.[5][6][1]

paras: In pectus excavatum the sternum and adjacent costal cartilages are displaced inward, and the lower ribs can flare outward; chest and back pain are common and usually musculoskeletal. In mild cases heart and lung function are normal, while severe cases can compress the heart and reduce exercise capacity.[3][2] Pectus carinatum is an outward protrusion or tilt of the sternum; a 2024 review notes it has potential psychological impact but no demonstrated physiologic impact, and describes the related pectus arcuatum as a short, fused sternum with a high protrusion.[1]

Both shapes are linked in some patients to connective tissue syndromes such as Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos and Noonan syndromes.[3] Patients may feel embarrassment or avoid shirtless activities, which is a common reason cosmetic correction is sought.[3]

For carinatum in patients with a flexible chest wall who adhere to a bracing programme, a 2024 review reports non-operative compression bracing is successful.[1] Wikipedia notes that treatment typically runs from six months to two years and that a 2012 American Pediatric Surgical Association guideline supports bracing as first-line.[7] For excavatum, a suction device called a vacuum bell (introduced in 2006) lifts the sternum; results vary and long-term data are limited.[3]

The Ravitch procedure, described by Mark Ravitch in 1949, is an open repair; the Nuss procedure places a curved bar under the sternum through small side incisions and flips it to push the sternum outward, with the bar typically removed after about two years.[3][6][5] Donald Nuss's 1998 report described 42 young patients treated without cartilage incision or resection, and a later review described 21 years of experience in 1,215 patients.[5][8] For carinatum, the Ravitch or a reverse Nuss are the common surgical options when bracing is unsuitable or fails.[7]
A multicentre FDA-sponsored trial examined a magnetic 'mini-mover' device for excavatum.[9] Other published variants include external distraction and extrathoracic traction methods.[3]

Custom silicone chest implants can reshape the contour cosmetically but do not treat cardiac or respiratory effects, and fat grafting can fill small residual defects.[3] Two small registered studies (7 and 10 participants) have tested camouflage approaches for excavatum.[10][11]

Surgical research on pectus repair is extensive. Nuss's 10-year review of a minimally invasive operation requiring neither cartilage incision nor resection, which has been cited more than 700 times, covered 148 evaluated patients and 42 children under 15 treated with the technique.[5] A pectus index from CT of 3.25 was reported in a 1987 preliminary report to separate patients who needed surgery from matched controls.[12] A review of 1,215 patients over 21 years described long-term experience with the Nuss procedure.[8]

Recent trials concern the recovery side: a 2026 randomized trial of scheduled ibuprofen with diclofenac suppository after the Nuss procedure in children found lower pain scores at 6 to 24 hours and lower opioid use than on-demand dosing;[13] a randomized trial compared erector spinae plane block with thoracic paravertebral block for analgesia after Nuss repair;[14] and another trial tested cryoanalgesia after repair.[15] A controlled study of aggressive respiratory rehabilitation after Nuss repair examined whether it improved inspired volumes.[16]

Early complications after the Nuss procedure can include pneumothorax, which often resolves on its own, and relapse is a concern after some open techniques.[3] Pain control after repair is a major clinical focus, as shown by the several analgesia trials above.[13][14][15] Braces require daily wear for months and rely on family support and adherence.[7]

Chest wall shape appears in looksmax.org threads on carinatum alternatives to surgery, on excavatum, and on long guides that propose exercise and posture work as correction; people also discuss it on T Nation bodybuilding forums where users ask about jutting or concave sternums.[17][18][19][20] Clinical reviews describe exercise as a supportive part of conservative management for excavatum rather than a substitute for bracing or surgery.[3]
